chapters.title: Chapter 3: Energy, Commodities, and Global Chokepoints

lessons.title: Case Study: The 2022-23 Energy Price Shock and Its Impact on the Rupee and the Nifty

body.text: The first week of the Russia-Ukraine war was a shock. The year that followed was a slow grind, a weakening rupee, a record RBI hiking cycle, and a Nifty that, against most expectations, ended 2022 barely changed. This is what a channel plays out like once you stop watching day by day.

children.text: Chapter 1's case study covered the first week after Russia's invasion of Ukraine. This case study zooms out to the full year that followed, when the energy shock stopped being a single headline and became a sustained economic pressure the RBI and Indian markets had to live with for months. Tracking the whole arc reveals something the first-week view could not: which parts of the four-channel framework mattered most over time, and a genuinely surprising twist in how the Nifty actually held up.

stats.label: RBI repo rate
stats.context: The cumulative rise from May 2022 to February 2023, across an unscheduled hike and several regular policy meetings, one of the fastest tightening cycles in the RBI's recent history

stats.label: The rupee
stats.context: First breaching 80 against the US dollar in July 2022, and weakening further to record lows later in the year, as the energy-driven current account pressure combined with a broadly stronger dollar globally

stats.label: Nifty, calendar year 2022
stats.value: Ended with a modest single-digit gain
stats.context: A genuinely surprising outcome given the scale of the shock, and notably better than most major global equity indices that year

children.text: The FII vs DII Story: Why the Nifty Didn't Crash

This is the part of the story that most surprises people who only remember 2022 as a year of war, inflation, and rate hikes. Foreign institutional investors were large net sellers of Indian equities that year, a record annual net outflow at the time, widely reported in the range of $15 to 17 billion, consistent with the capital flows channel from Chapter 1 during a global risk-off period. But domestic institutional investors, mutual funds and insurance companies buying largely on behalf of ordinary Indian retail investors, were large net buyers over the same period, more than offsetting the FII outflow.

body.title: Two Opposing Flows in the Same Market, Same Year

columns.label: FIIs (foreign institutional investors)
points: Large net sellers of Indian equities through 2022
Reacting to a global risk-off mood, rising US rates, and a stronger dollar pulling capital back toward developed markets
Consistent with the capital flows channel behaving exactly as this course would predict

columns.label: DIIs (domestic institutional investors)
points: Large net buyers of Indian equities over the same period
Fuelled substantially by growing retail participation through mutual fund SIPs, a structural, multi-year trend rather than a one-off
Acted as a genuine offsetting cushion, something the simple 'FII selling equals market falls' version of the story misses entirely

body.text: This is the most important nuance in this case study. The capital flows channel is real, but it is not the whole picture in a market with a large and growing domestic investor base. India's rising SIP culture has become a structural buffer against foreign outflows in a way that was far less true a decade earlier, and that buffer is itself worth tracking as a standalone indicator.

children.text: The Rupee's Year: RBI Intervention and Falling Reserves

While the Nifty found its offsetting buyer, the rupee had no equivalent cushion. It weakened steadily through 2022, pressured by the wider current account deficit from costlier energy imports and by a broadly strengthening US dollar as the US Federal Reserve raised its own rates aggressively. The RBI intervened repeatedly, selling dollars from its foreign exchange reserves to slow the pace of the rupee's decline, consistent with its stated approach of managing volatility rather than defending any specific level. India's forex reserves fell meaningfully over the year, though this reflected both RBI's dollar sales and valuation effects, as a stronger dollar reduced the dollar-value of the non-dollar assets held within those reserves, not intervention alone.

body.title: Explaining the Surprising Resilience
body.scenario: A friend who only follows headlines is confused: 'There was a war, oil spiked, the RBI hiked rates nine times in a year, and the rupee hit record lows, so why didn't the Nifty crash in 2022?'
body.prompt: Using what you've learned in this case study, explain the resilience in your own words.
body.modelAnswer: The Nifty faced real pressure from the capital flows channel, FIIs were large net sellers that year, consistent with a global risk-off mood and rising US rates pulling money back to developed markets. But India's own domestic institutional investors, largely channelling growing retail SIP flows, were large net buyers over the same period, more than offsetting the FII selling. The rupee, which did not have an equivalent domestic offsetting flow, weakened much more visibly instead, absorbing more of the pressure from the energy shock and the stronger dollar than equities did.

body.title: What Offset FII Selling in 2022?
body.question: Despite large FII net selling in 2022, the Nifty ended the year only modestly changed. What was the main domestic factor that helped offset this?
options: The RBI directly buying Nifty stocks
Large net buying from domestic institutional investors, fuelled substantially by retail mutual fund SIP flows
A government ban on further FII selling
Falling crude oil prices throughout the year
body.explanation: Domestic institutional investors, largely channelling retail mutual fund flows including SIPs, were large net buyers through 2022, offsetting a substantial share of the FII outflow. Crude prices remained elevated for much of the year rather than falling, and the RBI does not buy equities as a policy tool.

points: The 2022-23 energy shock played out as a sustained, multi-month pressure rather than a single event, visible in a rapid RBI hiking cycle from roughly 4% to 6.5% and a rupee that crossed both 80 and later 83 to the dollar
FIIs were large net sellers of Indian equities in 2022, a record annual outflow at the time, consistent with the capital flows channel during a global risk-off period

Domestic institutional investors, powered substantially by India's growing retail SIP culture, were large net buyers over the same period, offsetting much of the FII selling and helping the Nifty end the year only modestly changed
The rupee absorbed more visible pressure than equities did, since it lacked an equivalent domestic offsetting flow, and the RBI's reserve intervention slowed but did not fully prevent its decline

The key lesson: a channel from this course's framework, like capital flows, is real, but its market impact can be significantly cushioned or amplified by structural domestic factors that have nothing to do with the original geopolitical event itself
